**Becquerel** is a [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_craters "Lunar craters") [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") that lies in the northern [hemisphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere "Sphere") on the [far side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_side_(Moon) "Far side (Moon)") of the [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon "Moon").[[2]](#cite_note-Byrne_2008-2) This is an ancient and heavily worn formation that is now little more than an irregular depression in the surface. The outer rim has been worn and reshaped until it forms a rugged, mountainous region around the flatter interior.

The most notable of the formations on the rim is Becquerel X, which is part of a double crater along the northwestern rim. There is a short valley paralleling the southwestern rim, most likely formed by the merging of several small craters. The interior floor of Becquerel is relatively flat, but with rough sections and several tiny craterlets marking the surface. There is a dark patch (low [albedo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albedo "Albedo")) on the floor near the southern rim.[[3]](#cite_note-Bussey_Spudis_2004-3): 30–31

To the west of Becquerel are [H. G. Wells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._G._Wells_(crater) "H. G. Wells (crater)") and [Tesla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tesla_(crater) "Tesla (crater)"), to the north is [Segers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Segers_(crater) "Segers (crater)"), to the northeast is [Bridgman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridgman_(crater) "Bridgman (crater)"), and to the south is [Van Maanen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Maanen_(crater) "Van Maanen (crater)").[[4]](#cite_note-LAC_30-31-4)

This crater is named after French physicist [A. Henri Becquerel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Becquerel "Henri Becquerel") (1852–1908),[[5]](#cite_note-Menzel_et_al_1971-5) a 1903 [Nobel laureate in Physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physics "Nobel Prize in Physics"). Its designation was formally adopted by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") in 1970.[[1]](#cite_note-GPN-1)
